The selected publications were examined in terms of publication year, geographical distribution, research methods, AI technologies employed, and application areas. The findings indicate that research on artificial intelligence in higher education has increased substantially in recent years, with intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, and automated assessment tools emerging as the most frequently studied applications. The results reveal that AI applications contribute to personalized learning experiences, improve administrative efficiency, and support early identification of at-risk students. However, the analysis also identifies significant gaps, including limited theoretical grounding, insufficient attention to ethical considerations, and a scarcity of studies examining long-term learning outcomes. Furthermore, most research originates from a small number of countries, suggesting a need for broader geographical representation. The study concludes that although artificial intelligence holds considerable promise for transforming higher education, future research should address pedagogical integration, ethical frameworks, and educator readiness. Implications for researchers, practitioners, and policymakers are discussed.

This study aims to examine student perceptions regarding the importance of engagement strategies in online courses. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected through a survey administered to undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in online programs at a public university. The survey instrument addressed three categories of engagement strategies: learner-to-learner, learner-to-instructor, and learner-to-content. Descriptive statistics and inferential analyses were used to identify which strategies students perceived as most valuable. The findings indicate that students rated learner-to-instructor engagement strategies as the most important, particularly timely feedback, regular announcements, and instructor presence in discussions. Learner-to-content strategies, including interactive multimedia and authentic tasks, were also valued highly, whereas learner-to-learner strategies received comparatively lower importance ratings. Additional analyses revealed that perceptions varied according to students' prior online learning experience and enrollment status. The results suggest that instructor visibility and structured content interaction play a central role in fostering perceived engagement in online environments. The study concludes that online course designers should prioritize instructor-driven communication and meaningful content interaction while carefully structuring collaborative activities. These findings offer practical guidance for faculty and instructional designers seeking to improve engagement and retention in online higher education.

This study aims to map the research landscape of student engagement and educational technology in higher education through a systematic mapping review. Peer-reviewed empirical studies published in indexed journals were identified through comprehensive database searches, and studies meeting predefined inclusion criteria were coded and analyzed. The corpus was examined with respect to publication trends, geographical distribution, methodological approaches, technology types, and the dimensions of engagement addressed. The findings reveal a marked increase in publications over the past decade, with quantitative survey designs dominating the field. Learning management systems, social media, and mobile technologies were the most frequently investigated tools, while behavioral engagement received considerably more attention than emotional and cognitive dimensions. The analysis also shows that most studies were conducted in a limited set of countries and disciplines, and that theoretical frameworks of engagement were often applied superficially or inconsistently. The results highlight substantial gaps concerning longitudinal designs, underrepresented regions, and the integration of multidimensional engagement models. The study concludes that future research should adopt more rigorous conceptualizations of engagement, diversify methodological approaches, and examine emerging technologies. The mapping provides researchers and practitioners with an evidence-based overview to guide subsequent empirical work and technology-supported pedagogical design in higher education.

This study aims to investigate the impact of artificial intelligence on learner-instructor interaction in online learning environments. A qualitative research design was adopted, and data were collected through semi-structured interviews with students and instructors who had experience with AI-supported online courses. Participants were asked about their perceptions of AI systems used for communication, feedback, and learning support. The interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence reshapes learner-instructor interaction in both supportive and constraining ways. Participants reported that AI tools enhanced the timeliness of feedback, enabled continuous learning support, and reduced instructors' repetitive workload, thereby allowing more time for meaningful pedagogical engagement. However, concerns were raised regarding the potential erosion of personal connection, ambiguity about the boundary between human and automated responses, and risks related to privacy and surveillance. Students expressed a preference for AI systems that complement rather than replace instructor presence. The results suggest that the perceived quality of interaction depends on transparency, trust, and the appropriate division of roles between AI systems and instructors. The study concludes that successful integration of artificial intelligence in online learning requires deliberate design choices that preserve human relationships while leveraging automation for efficiency.

This study aims to review the literature on predicting academic success in higher education and to identify best practices in learning analytics applications. A systematic literature review was conducted, covering empirical studies that employed data-driven methods to predict student performance, retention, or dropout. The selected studies were analyzed in terms of data sources, predictive variables, analytical techniques, and reported outcomes. The findings show that demographic attributes, prior academic achievement, engagement indicators derived from learning management systems, and assessment data constitute the most commonly used predictors. Machine learning techniques, including decision trees, regression models, and neural networks, dominate the analytical landscape, with ensemble methods frequently achieving superior predictive accuracy. The review also reveals considerable variation in model transparency, validation practices, and the extent to which predictions are translated into pedagogical interventions. Ethical concerns, particularly regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, and student consent, remain insufficiently addressed in a substantial portion of the literature. The study concludes that effective prediction of academic success requires not only accurate models but also actionable feedback mechanisms, institutional support structures, and ethically grounded implementation frameworks. Recommendations are provided for researchers and higher education institutions seeking to develop responsible and pedagogically meaningful learning analytics systems.

This study aims to examine the effectiveness of an adaptive e-learning environment based on learning styles and its impact on the development of students' engagement skills. A quasi-experimental design with experimental and control groups was employed. The experimental group studied in an adaptive e-learning environment that presented content and activities tailored to students' identified learning styles, while the control group used a conventional, non-adaptive e-learning platform. Data were collected through an engagement scale administered before and after the intervention, supplemented by system log records. The findings indicate that students in the adaptive environment demonstrated significantly higher post-test engagement scores than their peers in the control group. Analysis of log data further revealed that learners in the adaptive condition spent more time on task, accessed a greater variety of learning resources, and completed more activities. The results suggest that aligning instructional content with learners' preferences enhances behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions of engagement. The study concludes that adaptive e-learning environments constitute a promising approach for fostering sustained learner involvement in online settings. Implications for instructional designers include the importance of learner modeling, flexible content sequencing, and continuous adaptation mechanisms in the design of personalized digital learning environments.

This study aims to explore the experiences and approaches of faculty members and administrators in the United States during the early weeks of the transition to emergency remote teaching caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. A survey-based research design was employed, and data were collected from faculty and administrators representing institutions of varying types and sizes. The questionnaire addressed instructional adjustments, institutional support, technology use, and perceived challenges. Quantitative responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings reveal that the majority of faculty had limited prior experience with online teaching and relied heavily on synchronous video conferencing to replicate classroom instruction. Institutions rapidly expanded technological support and instructional design assistance, yet respondents reported substantial variation in the adequacy of these resources. Faculty expressed concerns regarding student access to technology, academic integrity, assessment adaptation, and workload intensification. Administrators emphasized crisis communication, policy flexibility, and equity considerations. The results indicate that the abrupt transition exposed pre-existing gaps in institutional readiness for online education while also accelerating the adoption of digital pedagogies. The study concludes that sustained investment in faculty development, flexible policies, and resilient infrastructure is essential for preparing higher education institutions for future disruptions.

This study aims to provide a systematic literature review of the terminology used to describe personalized learning in educational research. Given the proliferation of overlapping concepts such as adaptive learning, individualized instruction, and differentiated learning, the review seeks to clarify definitional boundaries and usage patterns. Peer-reviewed publications were retrieved from major academic databases and screened according to predefined inclusion criteria. The selected studies were coded with respect to the terms employed, their explicit definitions, theoretical foundations, and technological contexts. The findings reveal considerable terminological inconsistency across the literature. Many studies use personalized learning interchangeably with related terms without providing explicit definitions, while others assign divergent meanings to identical concepts. The analysis identifies recurring definitional dimensions, including learner control, content adaptation, pace adjustment, and goal orientation, which distinguish the various terms. Technology-oriented studies tend to emphasize algorithmic adaptation, whereas pedagogically oriented studies foreground learner agency and instructional flexibility. The results suggest that conceptual ambiguity impedes cumulative knowledge building, complicates cross-study comparison, and weakens the design of empirical investigations. The study concludes by proposing a structured terminological framework that situates personalized learning and its related terms along explicit dimensions, offering researchers and practitioners a common vocabulary for future scholarship and implementation.

This study aims to investigate the impact of gamification on students' learning, engagement, and behavior. A quasi-experimental design was implemented in an undergraduate course, in which the experimental group participated in a gamified learning environment incorporating points, badges, leaderboards, and progress indicators, while the control group followed the same curriculum without game elements. Data were collected through achievement tests, an engagement questionnaire, and behavioral records extracted from the learning platform. The findings indicate that students in the gamified condition achieved significantly higher learning outcomes and reported greater levels of engagement compared with the control group. Behavioral data revealed increased frequency of platform logins, higher assignment completion rates, and more sustained participation throughout the semester in the gamified environment. The analysis further suggests that the motivational effects of gamification were strongest during the initial weeks and required careful design to be maintained over time. Individual differences, including prior achievement and competitiveness, moderated the effects of specific game elements. The study concludes that thoughtfully designed gamification can enhance learning and engagement in higher education, provided that game mechanics are aligned with pedagogical objectives rather than applied superficially. Practical recommendations are offered for instructors seeking to integrate gamified elements into their courses.

This study aims to explore the role of social media in collaborative learning within higher education. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered to university students who actively use social media platforms for academic purposes. The instrument measured social media use, interactivity with peers and instructors, collaborative learning, and perceived academic performance. The hypothesized relationships among these constructs were tested using structural equation modeling. The findings indicate that social media use has a significant positive effect on interactivity with peers and instructors, which in turn enhances collaborative learning. Collaborative learning was found to positively influence students' perceived academic performance and engagement. The results further reveal that ease of communication, resource sharing, and the immediacy of feedback constitute the primary mechanisms through which social media supports collaboration. However, the analysis also acknowledges potential drawbacks, including distraction and information overload, which may attenuate positive effects if usage is unregulated. The study concludes that social media, when purposefully integrated into instructional design, functions as an effective environment for collaborative knowledge construction in higher education. Implications are discussed for educators aiming to leverage social platforms to foster interaction, community building, and academically productive collaboration among students.

This study aims to conceptualize personalized adaptive learning as an emerging pedagogical approach enabled by smart learning environments. Drawing on a synthesis of the literature on personalization, adaptivity, and learning technologies, the paper develops a framework that integrates these strands into a coherent instructional model. The analysis distinguishes personalized learning, which emphasizes learner goals, preferences, and agency, from adaptive learning, which focuses on system-driven adjustment of content and support based on learner data. The proposed framework combines both perspectives, positioning smart learning environments as the technological infrastructure that enables continuous data collection, learner modeling, and real-time instructional adaptation. The findings of the conceptual analysis suggest that effective personalized adaptive learning requires four interdependent components: comprehensive learner profiles, flexible curriculum structures, data-driven adaptation mechanisms, and supportive learning analytics feedback for both learners and instructors. The paper further identifies key challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic transparency, teacher roles, and the risk of over-standardization. The study concludes that personalized adaptive learning represents a paradigm shift from uniform instruction toward learner-centered, data-informed education, while emphasizing that pedagogical principles must guide technological implementation. Directions for future research on the design and evaluation of smart learning environments are proposed.

This study aims to review content-based and context-based recommendation systems in technology-enhanced learning environments. A systematic review methodology was adopted, and relevant publications were retrieved from major digital libraries according to predefined search strings and inclusion criteria. The selected studies were classified with respect to recommendation techniques, data sources, application domains, and evaluation methods. The findings indicate that content-based approaches, which rely on item attributes and learner profiles, remain widely used due to their interpretability and independence from large user populations. Context-based approaches, incorporating situational factors such as location, time, device, and learner state, have gained increasing attention for their capacity to deliver situationally relevant recommendations. Hybrid systems combining collaborative, content-based, and contextual signals consistently outperform single-technique approaches in reported evaluations. The analysis also reveals persistent challenges, including the cold-start problem, data sparsity, limited standardization of evaluation metrics, and insufficient attention to pedagogical soundness of recommended resources. The study concludes that future research should focus on integrating pedagogical theories into recommendation logic, enhancing explainability for learners and educators, and developing benchmarking frameworks for fair comparison. The review provides researchers and developers with a structured overview to inform the design of effective educational recommendation systems.

This study aims to map the global landscape of emergency remote teaching in higher education during the first semester of the COVID-19 pandemic. A large-scale survey design was employed, gathering responses from higher education institutions across multiple countries and regions. The questionnaire addressed institutional responses, instructional delivery modes, technological infrastructure, support mechanisms, and challenges encountered during the transition. Data were analyzed descriptively and comparatively across regions and institution types. The findings reveal that the overwhelming majority of institutions shifted to online delivery within weeks, though considerable disparities emerged in technological readiness, faculty preparedness, and student access. Institutions in well-resourced contexts leveraged existing digital infrastructure, whereas those in developing regions faced significant connectivity and equipment constraints. Common challenges included assessment adaptation, practical and laboratory-based instruction, student engagement, and staff workload. The analysis also documents accelerated institutional innovation, including rapid faculty development programs, flexible academic policies, and expanded digital support services. The results underscore that the pandemic simultaneously exposed structural inequalities and catalyzed digital transformation in global higher education. The study concludes that lessons from this unprecedented semester should inform contingency planning, equitable technology policies, and the sustainable integration of online learning into post-pandemic educational strategies worldwide.

This study aims to develop an online engagement framework for higher education that synthesizes existing conceptualizations of student engagement into a practical model for online contexts. Drawing on a comprehensive review of engagement literature and established theoretical perspectives, the framework was constructed through iterative conceptual analysis and refined with reference to empirical studies of online learning. The proposed framework identifies multiple interrelated dimensions of online engagement, including behavioral, cognitive, emotional, collaborative, and social dimensions, and specifies observable indicators for each. The findings of the synthesis indicate that online engagement is a multidimensional and dynamic construct that cannot be adequately captured through participation metrics alone. The framework highlights the interplay between learner characteristics, instructional design, teaching presence, and institutional support in shaping engagement trajectories. Application scenarios demonstrate how the framework can guide course design, inform the interpretation of learning analytics data, and support targeted interventions for disengaged students. The study concludes that a structured, multidimensional understanding of engagement provides educators and researchers with a shared vocabulary and actionable reference points for enhancing online learning experiences. Recommendations are offered for validating the framework empirically and adapting it to diverse disciplinary and institutional contexts in higher education.

This study aims to develop a conceptual framework for learner engagement in blended learning environments. Recognizing that blended learning combines face-to-face and online components with distinct engagement dynamics, the framework was constructed through a systematic synthesis of engagement theory and empirical research on blended contexts. The analysis distinguishes behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement and examines how each dimension manifests across in-person and digital modalities. The findings of the conceptual synthesis indicate that engagement in blended environments is shaped by the interaction of learner factors, including self-regulation and technology readiness, with contextual factors such as course design coherence, teaching presence, and the integration quality between online and face-to-face components. The framework proposes that misalignment between modalities constitutes a primary source of disengagement, whereas deliberate pedagogical connection between components fosters sustained involvement. Indicators for assessing engagement in each modality are specified, offering a basis for both research operationalization and practical monitoring. The study concludes that engagement in blended learning should be conceptualized as an integrated, cross-modal phenomenon rather than as separate online and offline experiences. The framework provides researchers with a foundation for instrument development and offers practitioners guidance for designing blended courses that promote coherent and meaningful learner engagement.

This study aims to examine the strategies teachers employ to foster student engagement in blended learning environments. A qualitative multiple-case study design was adopted, involving teachers with substantial experience in delivering blended courses. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and analysis of course materials, and were examined using thematic analysis. The findings reveal that teachers deploy a repertoire of strategies spanning three domains: instructional design, relational practices, and technological facilitation. Within instructional design, teachers emphasized coherent integration of online and face-to-face activities, transparent expectations, and varied task formats. Relational strategies included establishing regular communication rhythms, providing personalized feedback, and cultivating a supportive learning community across modalities. Technological facilitation involved scaffolding students' use of digital tools and monitoring online participation data to identify disengagement early. The analysis further indicates that experienced teachers continuously adjust their strategies based on observed engagement cues, treating engagement as an ongoing pedagogical project rather than a fixed course property. Challenges reported include time constraints, uneven student digital competence, and institutional limitations. The study concludes that fostering engagement in blended environments requires deliberate orchestration across design, relationships, and technology. Implications are discussed for teacher professional development and institutional support of blended pedagogy.

This study aims to examine the potential of virtual worlds as a resource for hybrid education. Adopting a design-based research approach, the study implemented a virtual world environment as a complement to face-to-face and online instruction in a university course. Data were collected through student surveys, participation records within the virtual environment, and semi-structured interviews with participants and instructors. The findings indicate that the virtual world supported experiential and collaborative learning activities that were difficult to realize through conventional video conferencing, including simulations, spatial exploration, and embodied social interaction through avatars. Students reported heightened presence, increased motivation, and a stronger sense of community compared with standard online sessions. Participation data revealed sustained voluntary engagement beyond scheduled class times. However, the analysis also identified barriers, including technical requirements, initial orientation demands, and variation in students' spatial navigation skills. Instructors emphasized the need for careful pedagogical scripting to prevent novelty effects from overshadowing learning objectives. The study concludes that virtual worlds can meaningfully enrich hybrid education by providing immersive spaces for interaction and practice, provided that implementation is supported by adequate technical infrastructure and deliberate instructional design. Recommendations for integrating virtual environments into hybrid course structures are presented.

This study aims to examine how large-scale online learning was implemented to maintain educational continuity during the COVID-19 outbreak in China, focusing on the principles underlying disrupted classes and undisrupted learning. Employing a case study approach, the research analyzed national policy documents, platform usage data, and implementation reports associated with the nationwide transition to online education. The findings describe the rapid mobilization of cloud-based learning platforms, broadcast resources, and coordinated support mechanisms that enabled instruction for millions of students within weeks. The analysis identifies critical success factors, including government coordination, public-private collaboration in infrastructure provision, flexible pedagogical guidelines, and extensive teacher support initiatives. At the same time, the study documents substantial challenges, encompassing regional disparities in connectivity, variation in teacher readiness for online pedagogy, difficulties in sustaining student engagement, and concerns about screen time and assessment validity. The results suggest that emergency online education functioned as a viable stopgap while exposing systemic inequalities and pedagogical limitations of hastily transferred classroom practices. The study concludes that resilient education systems require sustained investment in digital infrastructure, teacher professional development, and flexible instructional models. Lessons drawn from this national experience offer guidance for education systems preparing for future large-scale disruptions.

This study aims to analyze scientific production and thematic evolution in the field of smart learning environments through a bibliometric approach. Publications indexed in major citation databases were retrieved using systematic search procedures, and the resulting corpus was analyzed with bibliometric techniques, including performance analysis, co-authorship mapping, keyword co-occurrence analysis, and thematic clustering. The findings reveal substantial growth in publication output over the examined period, with contributions concentrated in a limited number of countries and institutions. Co-authorship analysis indicates expanding international collaboration networks, although regional imbalances persist. Keyword analysis identifies dominant research themes, including learning analytics, adaptive systems, artificial intelligence in education, Internet of Things applications, and personalized learning, while emerging themes point toward immersive technologies and data-driven pedagogical design. The thematic mapping demonstrates a gradual shift from infrastructure-oriented research toward learner-centered and intelligence-augmented approaches. The analysis also identifies underexplored areas, notably ethical dimensions, teacher roles, and longitudinal evaluations of learning effectiveness. The study concludes that smart learning environments constitute a rapidly maturing research field whose future development depends on strengthening theoretical foundations, broadening geographical participation, and connecting technological innovation with rigorous pedagogical evidence. The results provide researchers with a structured overview of the field's intellectual landscape and development trajectories.

This study aims to develop a new model for utilizing online learning platforms to improve students' academic achievements and engagement. A design-based research methodology was employed across iterative cycles. In the first phase, factors influencing effective platform use were identified through a literature synthesis and needs analysis involving students and instructors. In the second phase, a structured usage model integrating instructional scaffolding, interactive content sequencing, formative feedback loops, and engagement monitoring was designed and implemented in undergraduate courses. The model's effectiveness was evaluated through a quasi-experimental comparison using achievement tests, an engagement scale, and platform analytics. The findings indicate that students taught according to the proposed model achieved significantly higher academic performance and demonstrated greater behavioral and emotional engagement than those using the platform in a conventional, unstructured manner. Analytics data corroborated these results, showing more frequent resource access, higher activity completion, and more evenly distributed study patterns in the experimental group. Interview data suggested that structured guidance and timely feedback were perceived as the model's most valuable components. The study concludes that the pedagogical structuring of online platform use, rather than platform availability alone, drives improvements in achievement and engagement. The validated model offers practitioners an actionable framework for technology-enhanced course design.

This study aims to define and conceptualize OER-enabled pedagogy as a distinct instructional approach grounded in the affordances of open educational resources. Through conceptual analysis, the paper examines how the permissions associated with open licensing, commonly summarized as the rights to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute, enable pedagogical practices that are impossible or impractical with conventionally copyrighted materials. The analysis develops a definitional framework specifying criteria for determining whether a given teaching practice constitutes OER-enabled pedagogy. Illustrative cases are presented, including renewable assignments in which students create, adapt, or improve openly licensed materials that retain value beyond the course. The findings of the conceptual work indicate that OER-enabled pedagogy shifts students from consumers to contributors of knowledge artifacts, potentially enhancing motivation, authenticity, and the social relevance of academic work. The framework distinguishes this approach from related constructs such as open pedagogy and open educational practices, addressing persistent terminological confusion in the literature. The study concludes that clear definitional boundaries are essential for cumulative research on the learning impacts of openness. Directions for future empirical investigation are proposed, including studies of student learning outcomes, instructor adoption factors, and institutional conditions that support the sustainable implementation of OER-enabled pedagogical practices.

This study aims to examine the effects of gender, educational level, and personality traits on online learning outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic. A quantitative research design was employed, and data were collected through an online survey administered to students participating in emergency remote education. The instrument included validated measures of personality dimensions, self-regulated learning behaviors, and perceived learning outcomes. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, group comparison tests, and regression analyses. The findings indicate that conscientiousness and openness were positively associated with perceived online learning outcomes, whereas neuroticism exhibited a negative relationship. Female students reported higher levels of self-regulation and engagement in online activities than male students, and significant differences in learning outcomes were observed across educational levels, with graduate students adapting more successfully than undergraduates. Regression results reveal that personality traits explained a substantial portion of variance in outcomes beyond demographic variables, with self-discipline and time management emerging as key mediating behaviors. The results suggest that individual differences meaningfully condition students' capacity to benefit from online learning under crisis conditions. The study concludes that institutions should provide differentiated support structures, including self-regulation training and targeted guidance for students whose characteristics place them at risk in autonomous online environments.

This study aims to investigate student perceptions of the gamification approach using Kahoot as a case study. A mixed-methods design was employed with undergraduate students who experienced Kahoot-based review activities throughout an academic semester. Quantitative data were collected through a questionnaire measuring perceived enjoyment, engagement, competition, and learning contribution, while qualitative data were obtained from open-ended responses and focus group discussions. The findings indicate that students held predominantly positive perceptions of Kahoot, describing the sessions as enjoyable, motivating, and effective for reinforcing course content. The competitive element was perceived as energizing by most participants, although a subset reported anxiety and discouragement associated with time pressure and public ranking. Students emphasized that immediate feedback helped them identify knowledge gaps and increased their attentiveness during preceding instruction. Qualitative analysis further revealed that the effectiveness of gamified sessions depended on question quality, appropriate difficulty, and moderation of competitive intensity. The results suggest that game-based response systems enhance classroom dynamics and formative assessment when implemented with pedagogical care. The study concludes that Kahoot constitutes a low-threshold, effective gamification tool for higher education, while recommending balanced use of competition, thoughtful question design, and attention to individual differences in students' responses to game elements.

This study aims to examine the key factors influencing college students' higher-order thinking skills in technology-supported learning environments. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from undergraduate students through validated scales measuring higher-order thinking, learning engagement, technology acceptance, self-efficacy, and perceived instructional support. Structural equation modeling was used to test the hypothesized relationships among these constructs. The findings indicate that learning engagement exerts the strongest direct effect on higher-order thinking skills, followed by academic self-efficacy and perceived instructional support. Technology acceptance influences higher-order thinking indirectly through its positive effect on engagement, suggesting that favorable attitudes toward technology translate into cognitive gains only when they foster active participation. Instructional support was found to strengthen both engagement and self-efficacy, underscoring the teacher's continuing centrality in technology-rich contexts. The model explained a substantial proportion of variance in higher-order thinking skills, and multi-group analyses indicated structural consistency across gender and disciplinary backgrounds. The results imply that cultivating higher-order thinking requires integrated attention to motivational, behavioral, and instructional factors rather than technology provision alone. The study concludes with practical recommendations for designing technology-supported learning experiences that deliberately promote analysis, evaluation, and creation through engaging tasks and sustained pedagogical scaffolding.

This study aims to examine how inquiry and critical thinking skills can be cultivated for the next generation of learners in an era shaped by artificial intelligence. Through an integrative review of research on inquiry-based learning, critical thinking development, and emerging intelligent technologies, the paper analyzes the evolving relationship between human reasoning skills and machine capabilities. The analysis argues that as artificial intelligence increasingly performs routine cognitive tasks, educational priorities must shift toward distinctly human competencies, including question formulation, evidence evaluation, assumption examination, and ethical judgment. The findings of the synthesis indicate that inquiry-based pedagogies, when systematically scaffolded, foster the epistemic practices underlying critical thinking, and that intelligent technologies can support this development by providing adaptive questioning, rich data environments, and immediate feedback. However, the review also identifies risks, including cognitive offloading, overreliance on algorithmic outputs, and diminished tolerance for intellectual struggle. A framework is proposed that positions artificial intelligence as an object of inquiry, a tool for inquiry, and a context demanding critical evaluation. The study concludes that preparing learners for an AI-mediated future requires curricula that deliberately integrate inquiry practices with critical examination of technology itself. Implications for curriculum design, teacher education, and educational policy are discussed.

This systematic review investigates the efficacy of educational technology (EdTech) in fostering student engagement within higher education, specifically focusing on the arts and humanities. The purpose was to synthesize existing empirical evidence to identify prevailing trends, effective strategies, and persistent challenges in this domain. A comprehensive search was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC databases, retrieving studies published between 2013 and 2023. Inclusion criteria mandated peer-reviewed articles reporting on EdTech interventions designed to enhance student engagement in arts and humanities higher education contexts. A total of 42 studies met the inclusion criteria and underwent thematic analysis. Findings indicate that interactive platforms, multimedia resources, and collaborative online tools significantly contribute to increased student participation, motivation, and perceived learning outcomes. Specific technologies such as virtual reality for historical simulations and digital storytelling tools for literary analysis emerged as particularly impactful. However, challenges related to digital literacy disparities, technological infrastructure, and faculty training were consistently identified. The review concludes that while EdTech holds substantial promise for enriching student engagement in the arts and humanities, its successful integration necessitates careful pedagogical design, robust institutional support, and continuous professional development for educators. Future research should explore long-term impacts and the nuances of engagement across diverse cultural and socio-economic contexts.

This study investigates students’ perceptions of distance education across multiple countries, aiming to identify commonalities and divergences in their experiences. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the research surveyed 5,487 university students from ten diverse nations, employing a validated questionnaire that assessed aspects such as technological infrastructure, pedagogical effectiveness, social interaction, and perceived learning outcomes. Subsequently, 120 semi-structured interviews were conducted with a subset of participants to gain deeper qualitative insights. Findings reveal a generally positive perception regarding the flexibility and accessibility of distance education, particularly among students in developing nations where physical access to higher education is often limited. However, significant challenges were also reported, including issues with internet connectivity, a perceived decline in the quality of social interaction, and difficulties in maintaining self-discipline. While most students appreciated the convenience, many expressed concerns about the effectiveness of online assessments and the lack of immediate feedback from instructors. The study concludes that while distance education offers substantial benefits, particularly in widening access, its successful implementation hinges on robust technological infrastructure, innovative pedagogical strategies that foster engagement, and comprehensive support systems to mitigate feelings of isolation and enhance academic integrity. These findings provide critical insights for policymakers and educators seeking to optimize distance learning environments globally.

This study investigates the multifaceted nature of the digital divide among higher education faculty, moving beyond simplistic access metrics to encompass disparities in digital literacy, pedagogical integration, and resource utilization. The purpose was to identify specific dimensions of this divide and their impact on teaching effectiveness and professional development. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a quantitative survey administered to 850 faculty members across diverse disciplines at five universities with qualitative semi-structured interviews conducted with a purposive sample of 40 faculty. Quantitative data were analyzed using ANOVA and regression to identify demographic correlates and predictive factors, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Findings reveal significant disparities based on age, disciplinary background, and institutional support structures. Younger faculty consistently demonstrated higher levels of digital proficiency and innovative technology integration, while humanities and social sciences faculty reported greater challenges compared to STEM colleagues. Crucially, a lack of targeted professional development and inadequate technical support emerged as primary inhibitors for effective technology use. The study concludes that the digital divide among higher education faculty is a complex issue requiring nuanced interventions beyond mere provision of hardware. Addressing this divide necessitates tailored training programs, robust institutional support, and a culture that fosters continuous digital skill development to ensure equitable opportunities for all faculty in the evolving digital academic landscape.

This study investigated the relationship between social presence and students' perceived learning and satisfaction in online higher education courses. The purpose was to understand how different dimensions of social presence contribute to these critical student outcomes. A quantitative research design employing a survey methodology was utilized, collecting data from 450 undergraduate students enrolled in fully online courses at a large public university. Social presence was measured using a validated instrument assessing affective, interactive, and cohesive dimensions, while perceived learning and satisfaction were measured through established scales. Regression analysis revealed a significant positive correlation between overall social presence and both perceived learning (β = 0.48, p < 0.001) and satisfaction (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). Specifically, the interactive and cohesive dimensions of social presence emerged as stronger predictors for both outcomes compared to the affective dimension. These findings suggest that fostering robust social interaction and a sense of community among online learners is paramount for enhancing their educational experience. The study concludes that instructors and instructional designers should prioritize strategies that actively promote student-to-student and student-to-instructor interactions and cultivate a strong sense of belonging to improve learning efficacy and overall student satisfaction in online learning environments.

This study explores the factors influencing university students' acceptance of Google Classroom as a learning management system, contributing to a deeper understanding of technology adoption in higher education. Drawing upon an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research aims to identify key determinants such as perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, social influence, and facilitating conditions that shape students' behavioral intention to use and actual system usage. A quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was employed, collecting data from 450 undergraduate students across various disciplines at a large public university. The Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) approach was utilized to analyze the proposed theoretical model and test the hypothesized relationships. Findings reveal that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use significantly predict students' behavioral intention to use Google Classroom, with perceived usefulness exerting a stronger influence. Furthermore, social influence and facilitating conditions were found to indirectly impact behavioral intention through their effects on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, respectively. Contrary to some previous studies, actual system usage was directly influenced by behavioral intention but not significantly by facilitating conditions. The study concludes that while the core TAM constructs remain robust predictors, the interplay of social and environmental factors is crucial for fostering technology acceptance in educational settings. These insights offer valuable implications for educators and policymakers seeking to optimize the integration and utilization of digital learning platforms.

This study investigated student satisfaction with online learning experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic, aiming to identify key factors influencing their perceptions. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a quantitative survey administered to 748 university students across various disciplines with qualitative data derived from 12 semi-structured interviews. The survey instrument assessed satisfaction across dimensions such as instructional design, technological support, instructor presence, and peer interaction using a five-point Likert scale. Qualitative data provided deeper insights into students' challenges and coping mechanisms. Findings revealed moderate overall satisfaction, with significant variations across specific dimensions. Students reported higher satisfaction with the flexibility and accessibility of online resources but expressed lower satisfaction regarding opportunities for meaningful peer interaction and the quality of synchronous online discussions. Technological issues, particularly internet connectivity and platform usability, emerged as significant detractors. The qualitative data further highlighted the importance of clear communication, empathetic instructor support, and effective time management strategies in mitigating negative experiences. In conclusion, while online learning provided continuity during the pandemic, enhancing student satisfaction necessitates targeted improvements in fostering a sense of community, refining interactive pedagogical approaches, and ensuring robust technological infrastructure and support. These findings offer valuable insights for designing more effective and engaging online learning environments in post-pandemic higher education.

This study investigated university faculty members' perceptions of their readiness to teach online, an increasingly critical skill in contemporary higher education. The primary purpose was to assess the various factors contributing to or hindering this perceived readiness. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a quantitative survey administered to 350 faculty members across three universities with qualitative data derived from 20 semi-structured interviews. The survey instrument measured perceived technological proficiency, pedagogical preparedness for online environments, institutional support, and self-efficacy. Findings revealed a significant disparity in perceived readiness, with younger faculty and those with prior online teaching experience reporting higher levels of preparedness. While most faculty expressed confidence in their subject matter expertise, many reported feeling inadequately trained in online pedagogical strategies and the effective use of learning management systems. Qualitative data highlighted a strong desire for more comprehensive professional development tailored to online teaching, alongside concerns regarding workload increases and equitable access to necessary technological resources. The study concludes that enhancing faculty readiness for online teaching requires multi-faceted institutional support, focusing on targeted pedagogical training, robust technical assistance, and explicit recognition of the additional effort involved. These findings offer valuable insights for universities seeking to strengthen their online learning capabilities.

This article provides a comprehensive state-of-the-art review of big data applications in education, aiming to delineate current trends, inherent limitations, and prospective research avenues. Employing a systematic literature review methodology, we analyzed 187 peer-reviewed articles published between 2013 and 2023 from Scopus and Web of Science databases, focusing on empirical studies and theoretical frameworks addressing big data in learning analytics, educational data mining, adaptive learning systems, and personalized education. The findings reveal a growing adoption of big data for predictive analytics of student performance, identification of at-risk students, and optimization of learning pathways. However, significant limitations persist, including ethical concerns regarding data privacy and algorithmic bias, challenges in data interoperability and integration across diverse educational platforms, and a lack of robust causal inference studies. Furthermore, the review highlights a notable gap in research exploring the impact of big data on pedagogical practices and teacher professional development. We conclude that while big data offers transformative potential for enhancing educational outcomes, future research must prioritize the development of ethical guidelines, standardized data governance frameworks, and rigorous methodologies to evaluate the causal impact of big data interventions. This includes focusing on explainable AI in educational contexts, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, and investigating the socio-technical implications of widespread big data adoption in education.

This study investigates the dual potential of digital higher education to act as either a divider or a bridge builder, as perceived by leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic. The purpose was to explore how university leaders conceptualized and operationalized educational technology (edtech) in response to the crisis, specifically examining its impact on access, equity, and the overall student experience. A qualitative research approach was employed, utilizing semi-structured interviews with 25 senior academic and administrative leaders from diverse higher education institutions across three continents. Thematic analysis revealed that leaders largely viewed edtech as a bridge builder, enabling continuity and expanding reach, particularly for remote and underserved populations. However, significant concerns were also identified regarding the exacerbation of existing digital divides due to unequal access to reliable internet and appropriate devices, and the varied digital literacy levels among students and staff. The findings highlight a tension between the aspirational goals of inclusivity and the practical challenges of implementation, underscoring the critical role of institutional policy and investment in mitigating inequalities. The study concludes that while edtech offers immense potential for fostering educational equity and accessibility, its realization is contingent upon proactive leadership that addresses infrastructural disparities and cultivates digital competencies, rather than assuming universal access and proficiency.

This study provides a comprehensive topic-based bibliometric analysis of smart learning research, mapping its intellectual landscape from inception to contemporary trends and future directions. The purpose was to systematically review the evolution of key research themes, identify influential works and authors, and forecast emerging areas within the smart learning domain. Utilizing a robust methodology, data was extracted from the Web of Science Core Collection, encompassing 4,872 articles published between 2005 and 2023. Co-occurrence network analysis of keywords and citation analysis were employed to identify prominent research clusters and their temporal shifts. Findings reveal a progression from early emphasis on ubiquitous computing and mobile learning to current focuses on artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and personalized adaptive learning environments. Three distinct phases were identified: foundational concepts (2005-2012), technological integration and application (2013-2018), and advanced pedagogical and data-driven approaches (2019-present). The analysis highlights a growing interdisciplinary nature and a shift towards learner-centric, data-informed intelligent systems. The conclusion underscores the transformative potential of smart learning, emphasizing the need for continued research into ethical AI integration, robust learning analytics frameworks, and the socio-technical implications for diverse educational contexts. This study offers valuable insights for researchers and practitioners, guiding future research agendas in this rapidly evolving field.

This study investigates the efficacy of pedagogical practices within fully online flipped classrooms in fostering learning performance amidst unpredictable times, such as the recent global pandemic. The primary purpose was to analyze the relationship between specific instructional strategies implemented in this modality and students' academic outcomes, along with their perceptions of learning effectiveness. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative analysis of student performance data (grades, completion rates) from 300 undergraduate students across three disciplines (n=100 per discipline) with qualitative data derived from student surveys and focus group discussions. Quantitative data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) to compare performance across different pedagogical interventions, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Findings indicate that a combination of pre-class asynchronous content engagement (e.g., interactive videos, simulations) and synchronous, instructor-led problem-solving sessions significantly correlated with higher learning performance and deeper conceptual understanding. Students reported increased engagement and autonomy, attributing their success to the flexibility and varied learning activities. The study concludes that fully online flipped classrooms, when strategically designed with diverse pre-class materials and interactive synchronous sessions, represent a robust and adaptable pedagogical model for maintaining and enhancing learning performance in unpredictable educational landscapes, effectively transitioning to a "new normal" of learning.

This study investigates the multifaceted impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics on higher education, employing a novel literature-based design fiction methodology. The purpose is to move beyond speculative predictions and instead ground future scenarios in existing academic discourse, thereby offering a more nuanced and evidence-informed understanding of potential transformations. A systematic review of peer-reviewed literature concerning AI, robotics, and higher education was conducted, identifying key themes, challenges, and opportunities. These emergent themes were then creatively synthesized into three distinct design fictions, each depicting a plausible future state of higher education under varying degrees of AI and robot integration. The fictions were subsequently analyzed to extrapolate commonalities and divergences in their implications for curriculum design, pedagogical practices, student learning outcomes, faculty roles, and institutional structures. Findings indicate a significant potential for AI and robots to personalize learning pathways, automate administrative tasks, and provide sophisticated analytical tools. However, the fictions also highlight critical challenges related to data privacy, ethical considerations of autonomous systems, the need for new digital literacies, and the potential for job displacement or skill obsolescence among educators. The study concludes that while AI and robotics offer transformative potential for higher education, proactive strategic planning, robust ethical frameworks, and continuous professional development are essential to harness their benefits while mitigating associated risks.

This study investigates the critical prerequisites for the successful integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in further education, focusing on the identification of key drivers, barriers, and viable business models employed by educational technology (EdTech) companies. The purpose is to provide a comprehensive framework that informs strategic planning and policy development for educational institutions considering AI adoption. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a systematic literature review of academic databases (Scopus, Web of Science) and industry reports with qualitative semi-structured interviews with 25 executives and product managers from leading EdTech companies specializing in AI solutions. Findings reveal that the primary drivers include enhanced personalized learning, administrative efficiency, and improved accessibility, while significant barriers encompass data privacy concerns, faculty resistance, high implementation costs, and the lack of robust digital infrastructure. Furthermore, three dominant business models emerged: subscription-based access to AI tools, partnership models with educational institutions, and API-driven integration services. The study concludes that successful AI integration necessitates a multi-faceted strategy addressing technological infrastructure, pedagogical redesign, ethical considerations, and sustainable financial models. Overcoming these challenges requires collaborative efforts between policymakers, educational leaders, and EdTech innovators to foster an environment conducive to AI-driven educational transformation.

This study investigates the efficacy of educational chatbots in enhancing learning outcomes within a project-based learning (PBL) framework, specifically for a team-based design course. The primary purpose was to assess the impact of chatbot integration on student performance, engagement, and perceived learning in comparison to traditional PBL methods. A quasi-experimental design was employed, involving 120 undergraduate engineering students across two cohorts. The experimental group (n=60) utilized an AI-powered chatbot designed to provide real-time feedback, facilitate knowledge acquisition, and offer collaborative support throughout their design projects. The control group (n=60) engaged in standard PBL activities without chatbot intervention. Data were collected through project grades, a validated learning outcomes questionnaire, and qualitative thematic analysis of student reflections. Findings indicate that students in the experimental group achieved significantly higher project grades (p < 0.01) and reported increased perceived learning effectiveness, particularly in problem-solving and critical thinking skills, compared to the control group. Qualitative data further revealed enhanced team collaboration and reduced cognitive load among chatbot users. The study concludes that educational chatbots can serve as valuable supplementary tools in PBL environments, fostering improved learning outcomes and enriching the student experience in complex, team-based design courses.

This study investigates the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance student performance monitoring and facilitate the proactive implementation of preventive measures in higher education. The primary purpose was to develop and evaluate an AI-driven framework capable of identifying students at risk of academic underperformance before significant issues manifest. Utilizing a robust dataset comprising historical academic records, engagement metrics, and demographic information from 10,000 university students over five academic years, a hybrid AI model was constructed. This model integrated a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network for sequential data analysis of academic progression and a Random Forest classifier for identifying critical contributing factors to academic decline. The methodology involved training, validation, and testing phases, with performance evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC metrics. Findings revealed that the AI model achieved a prediction accuracy of 89.5% in identifying at-risk students up to one month in advance, significantly outperforming traditional early warning systems. Key indicators identified included consistent drops in assignment scores, reduced LMS activity, and a decline in attendance. Based on these predictions, the system automatically suggested tailored interventions such as personalized tutoring referrals, academic counseling sessions, and peer mentoring programs. The conclusion posits that AI offers a highly effective and scalable solution for real-time student performance monitoring, enabling educational institutions to implement timely and targeted preventive measures, thereby improving student retention and academic success rates.

This study explores the multifaceted nature of online student engagement, aiming to understand the dynamic interplay of factors that shape students' experiences in virtual learning environments. Drawing upon a qualitative research design, the study employed semi-structured interviews with 25 undergraduate students enrolled in fully online programs at a large public university. Participants were selected through purposive sampling to ensure diversity in academic discipline and prior online learning experience. Thematic analysis, guided by a constructivist grounded theory approach, was utilized to identify recurring patterns and emergent themes within the interview data. Findings reveal that online student engagement is a complex balancing act, characterized by students navigating technological affordances and constraints, managing self-directed learning responsibilities, fostering instructor and peer interactions, and maintaining motivation amidst potential isolation. Key themes include the crucial role of instructor presence and pedagogical design in facilitating engagement, the challenges associated with maintaining focus and preventing procrastination, and the varying degrees to which students proactively seek out social and academic connections. The study concludes that effective online learning environments necessitate a holistic approach that not only leverages technological tools but also strategically cultivates a sense of community, provides clear structural support, and empowers students with self-regulation strategies to navigate the unique demands of online learning.

This study investigates the transformative impact of online learning platforms (OLPs) on the structural and pedagogical frameworks of modern higher education. The primary purpose is to analyze how the widespread adoption of OLPs has necessitated a fundamental reconstruction of traditional educational models, examining both the opportunities and challenges presented. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a quantitative analysis of student enrollment and completion rates across various OLP models (MOOCs, blended learning, fully online degrees) with qualitative data derived from semi-structured interviews with university administrators, faculty, and students (n=60) at five institutions leveraging OLPs extensively. Findings indicate a significant shift towards more flexible, accessible, and personalized learning pathways, with OLPs facilitating broader student demographics and promoting competency-based learning modules. However, challenges related to digital equity, faculty training, and maintaining academic rigor in virtual environments were also prominent. The study concludes that OLPs are not merely supplementary tools but fundamental drivers reshaping curriculum design, assessment strategies, and institutional infrastructure, compelling higher education to adapt proactively to a digitally integrated future while addressing persistent equity gaps.

This study investigated the efficacy of a chatbot-based intervention for improving Spanish punctuation skills and its broader impact on fostering open and flexible learning environments. The purpose was to address common challenges in Spanish punctuation acquisition among university students and to explore the potential of conversational AI as a pedagogical tool within modern educational paradigms. A quasi-experimental design was employed, involving 120 undergraduate students divided into an experimental group utilizing the chatbot for self-directed practice and a control group receiving traditional instruction. Pre- and post-intervention assessments measured punctuation proficiency, while student surveys and qualitative feedback explored perceptions of learning flexibility and engagement. Findings revealed a statistically significant improvement in punctuation scores for the experimental group compared to the control group (p < 0.01), indicating the chatbot's effectiveness in facilitating targeted skill development. Furthermore, qualitative data highlighted increased student autonomy, enhanced motivation through immediate feedback, and a perception of greater flexibility in accessing learning resources, aligning with principles of open and flexible learning. The study concludes that chatbots represent a valuable and adaptable tool for enhancing specific language skills like punctuation and contribute significantly to creating more accessible, personalized, and engaging learning experiences that support the evolution towards open and flexible educational models.

This study investigated the predictive power of synchronous and asynchronous class attendance on academic success in online higher education. The primary purpose was to determine the distinct contributions of each attendance mode to overall academic performance, measured by final course grades. A quantitative, correlational research design was employed, analyzing data from 2,548 students across 12 fully online courses at a large public university during the 2022-2023 academic year. Attendance data, meticulously logged by the learning management system, categorized participation as either live synchronous session attendance or engagement with asynchronous materials (e.g., recorded lectures, discussion board posts). Multiple linear regression analysis was utilized to model the relationship between attendance variables and academic outcomes, controlling for demographic factors such as prior GPA and student classification. Findings revealed that both synchronous and asynchronous attendance were significant positive predictors of academic success. However, synchronous attendance exhibited a slightly stronger unique predictive effect (β = 0.38, p < .001) compared to asynchronous engagement (β = 0.31, p < .001), indicating that real-time interaction may offer marginal additional benefits. The study concludes that while flexible asynchronous learning is valuable, encouraging synchronous participation could further enhance student achievement in online environments. These insights are crucial for optimizing instructional design and support strategies in online education.

This study investigated the technology acceptance of four distinct digital learning technologies—classroom response systems (CRS), classroom chat, e-lectures, and mobile virtual reality (MVR)—among university students after three months of consistent usage. The primary purpose was to assess the sustained acceptance levels and identify the underlying factors influencing perceived usefulness and ease of use for each technology. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative survey data from 450 students across multiple disciplines with qualitative insights derived from 30 semi-structured interviews. The survey utilized an adapted Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) model, measuring performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, and habit. Findings revealed significant differences in acceptance levels across the four technologies. E-lectures demonstrated the highest sustained acceptance, primarily driven by perceived usefulness and compatibility with existing study habits. CRS showed moderate acceptance, influenced by immediate feedback utility but occasionally hindered by technical glitches. Classroom chat exhibited lower acceptance, often perceived as distracting rather than facilitative for learning. MVR, despite high initial hedonic motivation, faced challenges related to effort expectancy and technical accessibility, impacting long-term acceptance. The study concludes that sustained technology acceptance in digital learning environments is a complex interplay of functional utility, user experience, and integration into established learning routines, with significant variations across different technological affordances.

This systematic review synthesizes extant literature on online Communities of Inquiry (CoI), focusing on the interplay and challenges associated with social, cognitive, and teaching presences. The primary purpose was to identify recurring issues and effective strategies in fostering these presences within online learning environments, thereby informing pedagogical practices and technological design. A comprehensive search of academic databases (Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC) was conducted for peer-reviewed articles published between 2013 and 2023, yielding 78 relevant studies. Qualitative content analysis was employed to extract and synthesize findings related to the conceptualization, manifestation, and interrelationships of the three presences. Key findings indicate that while cognitive presence is often the most explicitly targeted, its effective development is heavily reliant on robust social and teaching presences, which frequently present the most significant challenges. Issues include a lack of perceived connection among learners (social presence), difficulties in facilitating deep critical discourse (cognitive presence), and inadequate instructor guidance or feedback (teaching presence). The review concludes that a holistic approach, consciously integrating strategies to cultivate all three presences, is crucial for successful online CoI. Future research should explore dynamic models for assessing and enhancing these presences, particularly in diverse cultural and technological contexts.

This systematic literature review investigates the current state of accessibility within Open Educational Resources (OER) and Open Educational Practices (OOEP) for disabled learners. The purpose of this study was to synthesise existing research to identify prevalent accessibility issues, effective strategies, and gaps in the literature concerning the inclusive design and implementation of OER/OOEP. Following PRISMA guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar, yielding 47 peer-reviewed articles published between 2010 and 2023. Articles were critically appraised for relevance, methodology, and findings related to disability and OER/OOEP accessibility. The analysis revealed that while awareness of accessibility in OER/OOEP is growing, practical implementation remains inconsistent. Key findings indicate persistent challenges with technical accessibility (e.g., lack of alternative text, poor colour contrast, non-navigable interfaces), pedagogical accessibility (e.g., inflexible learning pathways, limited support for diverse learning needs), and policy-level integration. Conversely, studies highlighted promising practices such as co-creation with disabled learners, adoption of universal design for learning principles, and institutional commitment to accessible OER development. The conclusion underscores the urgent need for a more deliberate and comprehensive approach to embedding accessibility at every stage of OER/OOEP lifecycles, advocating for robust policy frameworks, developer training, and increased research into user-centred design methodologies to foster truly inclusive open education environments.

This study investigated the factors influencing online video usage and its impact on learning satisfaction among university students, extending the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The purpose was to identify key determinants beyond perceived usefulness and ease of use that contribute to students' engagement with educational videos and their subsequent satisfaction with the learning experience. A quantitative research design was employed, utilizing a structured questionnaire administered to a sample of 450 undergraduate students from diverse academic disciplines. The survey instrument measured constructs including perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, self-efficacy, instructor support, system quality, online video usage, and learning satisfaction. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to analyze the relationships between these variables. Findings revealed that perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and self-efficacy significantly predicted online video usage. Furthermore, instructor support and system quality were found to indirectly influence usage through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, respectively. Crucially, online video usage demonstrated a significant positive effect on learning satisfaction. The study concludes that while core TAM constructs remain vital, external factors like instructor support and system quality play a crucial role in shaping students' adoption of online videos, ultimately enhancing their learning satisfaction. These insights offer valuable implications for educators and instructional designers aiming to optimize the integration of online videos in higher education.

This study investigates the multifaceted factors influencing peer learning and subsequent academic performance within the asynchronous online discussion forums of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). Drawing upon a mixed-methods approach, the research first quantitatively analyzed discussion forum activity data from 1,247 participants across three distinct MOOCs, employing statistical correlation and regression analyses to identify relationships between participation metrics, interaction patterns, and final course grades. Subsequently, a qualitative thematic analysis of 86 purposively selected discussion threads and 28 semi-structured interviews with high and low-performing students provided deeper insights into perceived learning experiences, motivational drivers, and inhibitory factors. Key findings indicate that the quality and frequency of peer feedback, the perceived relevance of discussion prompts, and individual self-regulation strategies significantly predict peer learning engagement. Furthermore, a positive correlation was observed between the diversity of perspectives expressed within threads and improved performance, suggesting that exposure to varied viewpoints enhances cognitive processing. Conversely, factors such as delayed responses, lack of instructor presence, and perceived social loafing negatively impacted engagement and learning outcomes. The study concludes that fostering a supportive, interactive environment through carefully designed prompts, timely moderation, and explicit guidelines for constructive feedback is crucial for maximizing the benefits of peer learning in MOOC asynchronous forums and ultimately enhancing student performance.

This systematic review synthesizes empirical research on educational virtual reality (VR) games to identify prevailing trends in their design, application, and effectiveness. The purpose was to map the current landscape of research, pinpointing commonalities and gaps in the literature from 2018 to 2023. A rigorous search strategy was employed across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library, yielding 87 peer-reviewed articles that met predefined inclusion criteria. Data extraction focused on study design, VR game characteristics, learning outcomes measured, and participant demographics. Findings indicate a growing emphasis on immersive learning experiences for STEM subjects, with a significant proportion of studies employing quasi-experimental designs to compare VR interventions with traditional methods. Cognitive engagement and motivation were frequently reported as positive outcomes, although evidence for substantial improvements in long-term knowledge retention remains mixed. The most common VR game trends involved gamified simulations and interactive storytelling across K-12 and higher education settings. A notable trend is the increasing integration of haptic feedback and multi-user environments.
