Most faculty had little or no prior online teaching experience and leaned heavily on synchronous video conferencing to reproduce their classrooms. Institutions scaled up technical and instructional design support quickly, but respondents judged the adequacy of that support very differently. Faculty concerns clustered around student technology access, academic integrity, assessment, and a sharply increased workload. Administrators emphasized crisis communication, policy flexibility, and equity. The transition exposed gaps in institutional readiness that predated the pandemic, even as it accelerated the uptake of digital pedagogy. Responses came from institutions of varying types and sizes, which allowed the descriptive comparisons across institutional contexts reported here. If there is a lesson, it is that resilience cannot be improvised: sustained faculty development, flexible policies, and dependable infrastructure need to be in place before the next disruption arrives.

Personalized learning, adaptive learning, individualized instruction, differentiated learning: the terms multiply, but do they mean the same thing? This systematic review examines how such terminology is actually used. Peer-reviewed publications were retrieved from major databases, screened against inclusion criteria, and coded for the terms employed, their definitions, theoretical foundations, and technological contexts. Inconsistency is the rule. Many studies use personalized learning interchangeably with neighboring terms and never define it; others attach quite different meanings to the same word. Beneath the confusion, recurring definitional dimensions can be identified, notably learner control, content adaptation, pace adjustment, and goal orientation. Technology-oriented studies stress algorithmic adaptation, while pedagogically oriented work foregrounds learner agency. The cost of this ambiguity is real: findings cannot be compared across studies, knowledge does not accumulate, and study designs inherit the vagueness of their central construct. Coding captured each study's explicit definitions, theoretical foundations, and technological context, which made the definitional dimensions visible in the first place. We propose a structured framework that locates personalized learning and its relatives along explicit dimensions, giving researchers and practitioners a shared vocabulary to build on.

Does gamification actually change how students learn and behave, or does it merely decorate a course? We ran a quasi-experiment in an undergraduate course to find out. The experimental group worked in a gamified environment with points, badges, leaderboards, and progress indicators; the control group covered identical content without game elements. Achievement tests, an engagement questionnaire, and platform behavioral records provided the data. Students in the gamified condition scored significantly higher on achievement measures and reported stronger engagement. Their behavior differed too: more frequent logins, higher assignment completion, and steadier participation across the semester. Two caveats matter. The motivational lift was strongest in the opening weeks and faded without deliberate design attention, and individual differences, particularly prior achievement and competitiveness, moderated how students responded to specific game elements. Gamification can therefore improve learning and engagement in higher education, but only when its mechanics serve pedagogical goals rather than sitting on top of them. Achievement, questionnaire, and behavioral data thus told one consistent story from three independent measurement angles. Effect sizes were moderate across outcomes. We offer practical guidance for instructors considering the approach.

Social media is everywhere in students' lives; whether it supports serious collaborative learning is another question. We surveyed university students who use social platforms for academic purposes, measuring social media use, interactivity with peers and instructors, collaborative learning, and perceived academic performance, and tested the relationships with structural equation modeling. Social media use significantly increased interactivity with both peers and instructors, and that interactivity in turn strengthened collaborative learning. Collaborative learning was positively linked to perceived performance and engagement. Ease of communication, quick resource sharing, and immediate feedback appear to be the mechanisms doing the work. The risks are familiar, including distraction and information overload, and they can erode the benefits when use goes unmanaged. The overall conclusion is conditional rather than celebratory: purposefully integrated into instructional design, social media offers an effective environment for collaborative knowledge construction; left unstructured, its academic value is uncertain. The instrument was administered to students who already use these platforms academically, so the modeled paths reflect actual rather than hypothetical use. We discuss how educators can use these platforms to build interaction and community without importing their downsides.

Personalized learning and adaptive learning are often conflated, yet they rest on different logics: the first emphasizes learner goals, preferences, and agency, the second system-driven adjustment based on learner data. This conceptual paper brings the two together within smart learning environments. Synthesizing literature on personalization, adaptivity, and learning technologies, we develop a framework in which smart environments supply the infrastructure, namely continuous data collection, learner modeling, and real-time adaptation, on which personalized adaptive learning can operate. The analysis identifies four interdependent requirements: rich learner profiles, flexible curriculum structures, data-driven adaptation mechanisms, and analytics feedback serving both learners and instructors. It also names the difficulties honestly. Data privacy, algorithmic opacity, shifting teacher roles, and the danger of over-standardization all threaten the approach if left unexamined. Personalized adaptive learning marks a genuine shift from uniform instruction toward learner-centered, data-informed education, but technology must follow pedagogical principle rather than lead it. The synthesis drew on literature spanning personalization, adaptivity, and learning technologies rather than any single research strand. The paper closes with a research agenda for designing and evaluating smart learning environments on these terms.

Recommendation systems have become standard machinery in technology-enhanced learning, and two families dominate: content-based approaches built on item attributes and learner profiles, and context-based approaches that fold in situational signals such as location, time, device, and learner state. This systematic review takes stock of both. Publications from major digital libraries were selected against explicit criteria and classified by technique, data source, application domain, and evaluation method. Content-based systems remain popular for good reasons: they are interpretable and do not depend on large user populations. Context-aware systems are gaining ground because situational relevance matters in learning. Across reported evaluations, hybrids that combine collaborative, content, and contextual signals consistently beat single-technique systems. The unsolved problems are equally consistent: cold start, data sparsity, weakly standardized evaluation metrics, and, most troubling for education, scant attention to whether recommended resources are pedagogically sound. Future work should embed pedagogical theory in recommendation logic, make recommendations explainable to learners and teachers, and build benchmarking frameworks that allow fair comparison. The review offers researchers and developers a structured map for that agenda.

The first pandemic semester forced higher education online almost everywhere at once, creating a rare natural experiment. This study maps that global transition. Institutions across multiple countries and regions responded to a large-scale survey covering delivery modes, infrastructure, support mechanisms, and challenges; responses were analyzed descriptively and compared across regions and institution types. Nearly all institutions moved online within weeks, but the resemblance ends there. Well-resourced institutions leaned on existing digital infrastructure, while institutions in developing regions struggled with connectivity and equipment. Assessment, laboratory and practice-based teaching, student engagement, and staff workload emerged as shared pain points regardless of context. The crisis also accelerated innovation, visible in rapid faculty development programs, flexible academic policies, and expanded digital support services. The semester exposed structural inequalities and catalyzed digital transformation simultaneously, which is precisely why its lessons matter. The questionnaire covered institutional responses, delivery modes, infrastructure, support mechanisms, and challenges in a single instrument. Contingency planning, equitable technology policy, and the durable integration of online learning into ordinary provision should be built now, not reconstructed in the next emergency.

Participation metrics tell us who clicked, not who is engaged. This paper develops an online engagement framework for higher education that takes the difference seriously. Built through iterative conceptual analysis of the engagement literature and refined against empirical studies of online learning, the framework identifies behavioral, cognitive, emotional, collaborative, and social dimensions of engagement and specifies observable indicators for each. Engagement emerges from the synthesis as multidimensional and dynamic, shaped by the interplay of learner characteristics, instructional design, teaching presence, and institutional support rather than by any single factor. Application scenarios show the framework at work: guiding course design, disciplining the interpretation of learning analytics data, and targeting interventions at students whose disengagement would otherwise surface too late. A structured, shared understanding of engagement gives educators and researchers common reference points where loose talk of engagement currently prevails. The framework was refined iteratively against empirical studies of online learning rather than derived from theory alone. Empirical validation and adaptation to different disciplinary and institutional settings are the obvious next steps, and we outline how both might proceed.

Blended learning is routinely treated as two experiences stitched together, one online and one face-to-face. This paper argues for seeing learner engagement in blended environments as a single, cross-modal phenomenon and offers a conceptual framework built on that premise. Synthesizing engagement theory with empirical research on blended contexts, we trace how behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement manifest differently across in-person and digital components. Engagement turns out to be shaped by the interaction of learner factors, notably self-regulation and technology readiness, with contextual ones, including design coherence, teaching presence, and above all the quality of integration between modalities. Misalignment between the online and face-to-face parts of a course emerges as a primary source of disengagement; deliberate pedagogical connection between them sustains involvement. The framework specifies indicators for assessing engagement in each modality, usable for research operationalization and for practical monitoring alike. Indicators are specified separately for the online and face-to-face components, so the same dimension can be tracked across both. For researchers it offers a foundation for instrument development; for practitioners, guidance on designing blended courses whose parts actually cohere.

Experienced teachers do not leave engagement to chance, and blended courses give them two arenas to manage at once. This multiple-case study examines how such teachers foster student engagement in blended environments. Teachers with substantial blended teaching experience were studied through semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and course material analysis; the data were analyzed thematically. Their strategies fall into three domains. In instructional design, they wove online and face-to-face activities into a coherent whole, made expectations transparent, and varied task formats. Relationally, they kept regular communication rhythms, personalized their feedback, and built community across both modalities. On the technological side, they scaffolded students' tool use and watched participation data for early signs of drift. What distinguished these teachers most was their responsiveness: they read engagement cues continuously and adjusted, treating engagement as ongoing pedagogical work rather than a property a course either has or lacks. Time pressure, uneven student digital competence, and institutional constraints limited what they could do. Course material analysis corroborated what teachers described in interviews. Teacher development and institutional support for blended pedagogy should be designed with these realities in view.

Video conferencing keeps hybrid courses running, but it flattens much of what makes learning social. This design-based study asked whether a virtual world could restore some of that texture. A virtual world environment was implemented alongside face-to-face and online instruction in a university course; data came from student surveys, participation records inside the environment, and interviews with students and instructors. The environment enabled activities that ordinary video sessions could not carry, including simulations, spatial exploration, and embodied interaction through avatars. Students reported stronger presence, higher motivation, and a firmer sense of community, and participation logs showed voluntary engagement well beyond scheduled class times. The barriers were equally concrete: technical requirements, the time needed for initial orientation, and uneven spatial navigation skills. Instructors stressed that without careful pedagogical scripting, novelty threatens to eclipse learning objectives. Virtual worlds can genuinely enrich hybrid education as immersive spaces for interaction and practice, but only when infrastructure and deliberate instructional design carry their share of the load. Survey responses and participation records pointed in the same direction, which strengthens the interview findings. We close with recommendations for that integration.

When COVID-19 closed Chinese schools, the response was organized around a single principle: classes may be disrupted, learning must not be. This case study examines how that principle was implemented at national scale, drawing on policy documents, platform usage data, and implementation reports. Within weeks, cloud platforms, broadcast resources, and coordinated support structures were carrying instruction to millions of students. Several factors made this possible: strong government coordination, public-private cooperation on infrastructure, pedagogical guidelines flexible enough to fit local conditions, and extensive teacher support. The difficulties were just as instructive. Connectivity varied sharply by region, many teachers were unprepared for online pedagogy, student engagement proved hard to sustain, and concerns about screen time and assessment validity accumulated. Emergency online education worked as a stopgap while exposing systemic inequalities and the limits of classroom practices transferred hastily to screens. Policy documents, platform usage data, and implementation reports were triangulated throughout the analysis. The broader lesson is that resilient education systems are built in advance, through sustained investment in infrastructure, teacher development, and flexible instructional models, not assembled during the emergency itself.

How has research on smart learning environments developed, and where is it heading? This bibliometric study answers with data. Publications indexed in major citation databases were retrieved systematically and analyzed through performance analysis, co-authorship mapping, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic clustering. Output has grown substantially, though it remains concentrated in relatively few countries and institutions. International collaboration networks are expanding; regional imbalances persist nonetheless. Keyword analysis identifies the field's core themes, namely learning analytics, adaptive systems, artificial intelligence in education, Internet of Things applications, and personalized learning, with immersive technologies and data-driven pedagogical design emerging at the margins. The thematic map records a gradual shift from infrastructure-oriented work toward learner-centered, intelligence-augmented approaches. Three areas stand out as underexplored: ethics, teacher roles, and longitudinal evidence on learning effectiveness. Smart learning environments constitute a rapidly maturing field whose next phase depends on firmer theoretical foundations, broader geographical participation, and tighter coupling between technological innovation and pedagogical evidence. Performance analysis of output and citations complemented the network-based mapping. The analysis gives researchers a structured view of the field's intellectual landscape and its likely trajectories.

Making a learning platform available is easy; making it improve achievement is not. This design-based study developed and validated a model for the pedagogically structured use of online learning platforms. Iterative cycles began with a literature synthesis and a needs analysis involving students and instructors, from which a usage model was built around instructional scaffolding, interactive content sequencing, formative feedback loops, and engagement monitoring. The model was then implemented in undergraduate courses and evaluated quasi-experimentally with achievement tests, an engagement scale, and platform analytics. Students taught under the model outperformed peers who used the same platform in the conventional, unstructured way, and showed stronger behavioral and emotional engagement. Analytics corroborated the pattern: more frequent resource access, higher activity completion, and study time distributed more evenly across the term. In interviews, students credited the structured guidance and timely feedback above all else. The conclusion is pointed. Achievement gains come from the pedagogical structuring of platform use, not from platform availability. The needs analysis phase involved both students and instructors, anchoring the model's components in reported practice. The validated model gives practitioners an actionable framework for building that structure into technology-enhanced courses.

Open licensing grants five permissions, namely to retain, reuse, revise, remix, and redistribute, and those permissions make certain teaching practices possible that copyright forbids. This paper defines OER-enabled pedagogy as precisely that class of practices. Through conceptual analysis, we develop a definitional framework with criteria for judging whether a given practice qualifies. Renewable assignments illustrate the idea: students create, adapt, or improve openly licensed materials whose value outlives the course, in contrast to disposable assignments discarded after grading. The analysis suggests that OER-enabled pedagogy repositions students from consumers to contributors of knowledge artifacts, with plausible gains in motivation, authenticity, and the social relevance of academic work. The framework also disentangles OER-enabled pedagogy from open pedagogy and open educational practices, terms whose interchangeable use has muddied the literature. Definitional clarity is not pedantry; without it, research on the learning impacts of openness cannot accumulate. The five permissions are treated as the analytical core throughout, since each enabled practice traces back to at least one of them. We outline an empirical agenda covering student learning outcomes, instructor adoption factors, and the institutional conditions under which these practices become sustainable.

Emergency remote education tested every student, but not equally. This study asked how gender, educational level, and personality shaped online learning outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic. Students in emergency remote education completed an online survey with validated measures of personality, self-regulated learning, and perceived outcomes; the data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, group comparisons, and regression. Conscientiousness and openness predicted better perceived outcomes; neuroticism predicted worse. Female students reported more self-regulation and greater engagement in online activities than male students. Graduate students adapted more successfully than undergraduates. Notably, personality explained substantial variance in outcomes over and above demographics, with self-discipline and time management acting as the key mediating behaviors. Autonomous online environments, in other words, reward some dispositions and punish others, and under crisis conditions those differences widen. The survey instrument combined validated personality measures with self-regulated learning scales and perceived outcome items, allowing the mediation pattern to be tested directly rather than inferred. Institutions should respond with differentiated rather than uniform support: self-regulation training, structured guidance, and early attention to students whose characteristics put them at risk when learning moves online.

Kahoot has become a classroom fixture, but student experience of it is less uniform than its popularity suggests. This mixed-methods study examined student perceptions of the gamification approach through Kahoot-based review sessions run across a semester of undergraduate teaching. A questionnaire measured perceived enjoyment, engagement, competition, and learning contribution; open-ended responses and focus groups supplied the qualitative side. Perceptions were largely positive. Students found the sessions enjoyable and motivating, and credited immediate feedback with exposing knowledge gaps and sharpening their attention during the preceding instruction. Competition energized most participants, yet a distinct subset experienced anxiety and discouragement tied to time pressure and public ranking, a finding that complicates simple enthusiasm for leaderboards. Session quality depended on question design, appropriate difficulty, and how firmly the instructor moderated competitive intensity. Questionnaire scores and focus group accounts aligned closely, with the qualitative data explaining the minority pattern the numbers only hinted at. Kahoot works as a low-threshold, effective gamification tool for higher education, provided competition stays balanced, questions are crafted with care, and instructors remain alert to students who respond badly to being ranked in public.

Technology-rich classrooms do not automatically produce better thinkers. This study modeled the factors that actually influence college students' higher-order thinking skills in technology-supported environments. Undergraduates completed validated scales on higher-order thinking, engagement, technology acceptance, self-efficacy, and perceived instructional support; structural equation modeling tested the hypothesized relationships. Engagement exerted the strongest direct effect on higher-order thinking, with academic self-efficacy and instructional support following. Technology acceptance mattered only indirectly, through engagement: favorable attitudes toward technology translated into cognitive gains solely when they fostered active participation. Instructional support strengthened both engagement and self-efficacy, a reminder that teachers remain central even in heavily digital contexts. The model explained a substantial share of variance in higher-order thinking, and multi-group analyses held across gender and discipline. Cultivating analysis, evaluation, and creation therefore demands integrated attention to motivational, behavioral, and instructional factors; providing technology is the easy and insufficient part. All scales were validated instruments, and measurement checks preceded the structural analysis. Model fit indices met conventional thresholds. We close with recommendations for designing technology-supported learning that deliberately promotes higher-order thinking through engaging tasks and sustained pedagogical scaffolding.

As artificial intelligence absorbs routine cognitive work, the question of what schools should cultivate becomes sharper, and inquiry and critical thinking move to the center. This integrative review examines how those capacities can be developed in the next generation of learners. Drawing together research on inquiry-based learning, critical thinking development, and intelligent technologies, the analysis traces a shifting division of labor between human reasoning and machine capability. Distinctly human competencies, including question formulation, evidence evaluation, assumption examination, and ethical judgment, gain value precisely as machines take over the routine. The synthesis shows that systematically scaffolded inquiry pedagogies build the epistemic practices underlying critical thinking, and that intelligent tools can help through adaptive questioning, rich data environments, and immediate feedback. The risks run in parallel: cognitive offloading, overreliance on algorithmic outputs, and a shrinking tolerance for intellectual struggle. We propose a framework treating AI in three roles at once, namely as an object of inquiry, a tool for inquiry, and a context demanding critical evaluation. Preparing learners for an AI-mediated future means integrating inquiry practice with the critical examination of technology itself, with consequences for curriculum, teacher education, and policy.

Does educational technology actually deepen student engagement in the arts and humanities, fields often left out of the EdTech conversation? This systematic review synthesizes the evidence. Searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC covered 2013-2023; 42 peer-reviewed studies of EdTech interventions targeting engagement in arts and humanities higher education met the inclusion criteria and were analyzed thematically. Interactive platforms, multimedia resources, and collaborative online tools consistently raised participation, motivation, and perceived learning. Two applications stood out: virtual reality for historical simulations and digital storytelling for literary analysis. The recurring obstacles were equally clear, namely uneven digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and insufficient faculty training. EdTech holds real promise for these disciplines, but the promise is conditional. It depends on careful pedagogical design, solid institutional support, and continuing professional development for educators. The review followed a systematic protocol with predefined inclusion criteria, and thematic analysis was applied across the full set of 42 studies. Digital storytelling and VR cases were coded alongside more conventional platform interventions, which is what made the comparative pattern visible. Long-term impacts, and how engagement plays out across different cultural and socio-economic contexts, remain open questions for future research.

Students in ten countries, one question: how do they actually experience distance education? A validated questionnaire reached 5,487 university students across diverse nations, covering infrastructure, pedagogical effectiveness, social interaction, and perceived learning; 120 follow-up interviews added qualitative depth. Perceptions of flexibility and accessibility were broadly positive, especially in developing countries where physical access to higher education is constrained. The complaints were just as consistent: unreliable internet, thinner social interaction, and the struggle to maintain self-discipline. Convenience was appreciated almost everywhere, yet many students doubted the effectiveness of online assessment and missed immediate instructor feedback. Distance education clearly widens access. Whether it delivers on quality depends on conditions that vary sharply across contexts, including robust infrastructure, pedagogy that actively fosters engagement, and support systems that counter isolation and protect academic integrity. The questionnaire was validated before deployment, and the interview subsample was drawn to reflect the same national spread as the survey. Perceptions of assessment and feedback were probed separately from general satisfaction, which is why the convenience-effectiveness gap could be isolated. For policymakers and educators optimizing distance learning globally, those conditions, not the format itself, are where the work lies.

The digital divide among university faculty is usually measured by who has access to technology. That framing misses most of the problem. This study examined disparities in digital literacy, pedagogical integration, and resource use among 850 faculty members across five universities, pairing a survey (analyzed with ANOVA and regression) with interviews of 40 purposively selected academics. The divides run along several lines at once. Younger faculty showed higher proficiency and more innovative technology integration; humanities and social sciences faculty reported greater difficulty than STEM colleagues; and everywhere, the strongest inhibitors were the absence of targeted professional development and inadequate technical support. Hardware provision alone will not close gaps of this kind. What is needed is tailored training, dependable institutional support, and an academic culture that treats digital skill development as continuous rather than optional. The survey instrument covered digital literacy, pedagogical integration, and resource use as separate constructs, and ANOVA and regression analyses were run on each. The interview phase sampled across age groups, disciplines, and institutions purposively, so the qualitative accounts map onto the same divides the statistics identified rather than a convenience subset. Without those, the divide among faculty quietly reproduces itself in the classroom.

How much does feeling socially connected matter for what students think they learn online? We surveyed 450 undergraduates in fully online courses at a large public university, measuring social presence in its affective, interactive, and cohesive dimensions alongside perceived learning and satisfaction. Regression results were unambiguous. Overall social presence predicted both perceived learning (β = 0.48, p < 0.001) and satisfaction (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). The interactive and cohesive dimensions carried more weight than the affective dimension for both outcomes, which is a practically useful distinction: it is not warm feelings alone but actual interaction and a sense of group cohesion that move the needle. The implication for instructors and designers is concrete. The social presence instrument measured the affective, interactive, and cohesive dimensions separately, which is what allowed their relative weights to be compared. Controls for course type and prior online experience left the pattern intact. Prioritize structures that generate student-to-student and student-to-instructor exchange and that build belonging, because community in online courses is not an amenity; on this evidence, it is a condition of perceived learning itself.

Why do students adopt Google Classroom, and what actually drives their use? Working from an extended Technology Acceptance Model, this study surveyed 450 undergraduates across disciplines at a large public university and tested the model with PLS-SEM. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use both predicted behavioral intention, with usefulness the stronger of the two. Social influence and facilitating conditions mattered as well, but indirectly, working through usefulness and ease of use respectively. One result cut against parts of the prior literature: actual usage followed behavioral intention but was not significantly shaped by facilitating conditions. The core TAM constructs, in short, remain sturdy predictors, yet the social and environmental context around them decides how strongly they operate. The extended model added social influence and facilitating conditions to the classic TAM core, and PLS-SEM estimated direct and indirect paths simultaneously. Measurement validity checks preceded the structural model, and the sample spanned multiple disciplines to avoid a single-field bias. The indirect-only role of the contextual variables emerged from this full-path estimation, not from separate bivariate tests. For educators and policymakers rolling out learning management systems, the practical reading is that demonstrating genuine usefulness to students, and letting peer influence do its quiet work, will matter more than infrastructure checklists alone.

Online learning kept universities running during the pandemic; whether students were satisfied with it is a separate question. This mixed-methods study surveyed 748 university students across disciplines and interviewed twelve of them, measuring satisfaction with instructional design, technological support, instructor presence, and peer interaction. Overall satisfaction was moderate, with sharp variation underneath. Flexibility and access to online resources scored well. Peer interaction and the quality of synchronous discussions did not, and connectivity problems plus clunky platforms dragged perceptions down further. The interviews pointed to what helped: clear communication, instructors who responded with empathy, and workable time management strategies. Continuity, then, was achieved; satisfaction only partly so. Raising it requires deliberate work on community building, more genuinely interactive pedagogy, and infrastructure that does not get in the way. The satisfaction instrument distinguished instructional design, technological support, instructor presence, and peer interaction as separate dimensions, and the twelve interviewees were selected to span disciplines and satisfaction levels. That design is what allowed the moderate overall score to be decomposed into its strong and weak components. Those priorities are worth carrying into post-pandemic course design rather than treating the emergency semester as a closed chapter.

Feeling ready to teach online and being trained to do it are different things, and this study found faculty caught between them. A survey of 350 faculty members at three universities, plus twenty interviews, assessed perceived technological proficiency, pedagogical preparedness, institutional support, and self-efficacy. Readiness varied widely. Younger faculty and those with prior online teaching experience felt notably more prepared. Nearly everyone was confident in their subject matter; far fewer felt equipped with online pedagogical strategies or fluent in the learning management systems they were expected to use. The interviews added a consistent refrain: faculty want professional development built specifically for online teaching, and they want the extra workload acknowledged, along with fair access to the necessary technology. Building faculty readiness is therefore a multi-front task involving targeted pedagogical training, dependable technical assistance, and institutional recognition of the effort involved. The survey measured technological proficiency, pedagogical preparedness, institutional support, and self-efficacy as distinct constructs, and the twenty interviewees spanned all three universities. Interview themes mirrored the survey gaps closely. Universities that address only one front should not expect the others to take care of themselves.

Big data has been promised as education's next transformation for a decade. This state-of-the-art review asks what the research actually shows. We analyzed 187 peer-reviewed articles (2013-2023, Scopus and Web of Science) spanning learning analytics, educational data mining, adaptive systems, and personalized education. Adoption is real and growing, concentrated in predicting student performance, flagging at-risk students, and optimizing learning pathways. The limitations are just as established: unresolved ethical questions around privacy and algorithmic bias, poor data interoperability across platforms, and a striking shortage of studies capable of supporting causal claims. Research on what big data does to teaching practice and teacher professional development is thinner still. The transformative potential is plausible but unproven at the level of rigor the claims demand. The corpus was coded by application area, data type, analytical technique, and reported outcome, spanning learning analytics, educational data mining, adaptive systems, and personalized education as distinct strands. The decade-long window made the growth trajectory and its blind spots equally visible. Priorities for the field include ethical guidelines and data governance standards, methodologies built for causal inference, explainable AI in educational settings, and serious attention to the socio-technical consequences of adoption at scale.

Digital higher education can widen gaps or close them, and during COVID-19 university leaders had to decide, quickly, which it would do at their institutions. This qualitative study interviewed 25 senior academic and administrative leaders across three continents about how they conceptualized and deployed educational technology through the crisis. Most framed edtech as a bridge builder: it kept teaching alive and extended reach to remote and underserved students. Yet the same leaders described real fears about deepening divides, driven by unequal internet access, device shortages, and wide variation in digital literacy among students and staff. The tension between inclusive aspiration and practical constraint ran through nearly every account, and what separated better outcomes from worse was institutional policy and investment rather than technology itself. Edtech's potential for equity is genuine but conditional. The twenty-five leaders held senior academic and administrative roles and were interviewed during the crisis period itself, so the accounts capture decisions as they were being made. Thematic analysis traced the bridge-builder and divide-deepener framings across all three continents represented. It is realized by leadership that treats infrastructure disparities and digital competence as problems to be solved, not assumptions to be made.

Smart learning research has grown from a niche into a field; this bibliometric study maps how. Drawing 4,872 articles (2005-2023) from the Web of Science Core Collection, we applied keyword co-occurrence network analysis and citation analysis to trace research clusters and their shifts over time. The field's center of gravity has moved from ubiquitous computing and mobile learning toward artificial intelligence, big data analytics, and personalized adaptive environments. Three phases stand out: foundational concepts (2005-2012), technological integration and application (2013-2018), and advanced pedagogical, data-driven approaches (2019 onward). The trajectory is toward learner-centric, data-informed intelligent systems, with the field becoming steadily more interdisciplinary along the way. What the map also shows is where attention has not yet settled, notably ethical AI integration, robust learning analytics frameworks, and the socio-technical questions raised by intelligent systems in varied educational contexts. The 2005-2023 window and the Web of Science Core Collection source were fixed in advance, and keyword co-occurrence networks were built per phase to make the thematic shifts traceable. Citation analysis identified the field's anchor works alongside the cluster structure. For researchers and practitioners planning their next moves, those are the open territories.

The pandemic forced flipped classrooms fully online; this study asked whether the model still delivers under such conditions. Performance data from 300 undergraduates in three disciplines were analyzed with MANOVA to compare pedagogical approaches, while surveys and focus groups supplied the qualitative picture. The combination that worked was consistent: asynchronous pre-class engagement through interactive videos and simulations, followed by synchronous, instructor-led problem-solving sessions. Students taught this way performed better and showed deeper conceptual understanding, and they knew why, crediting the flexibility and the variety of learning activities for their increased engagement and autonomy. A fully online flipped classroom, strategically designed, is therefore not a compromise version of the face-to-face model but a robust pedagogical approach in its own right, and one suited to unpredictable circumstances. MANOVA compared the pedagogical approaches across the three disciplines simultaneously, and the survey and focus group data were collected from the same cohorts. The qualitative accounts thus explain the performance differences rather than merely accompanying them. As unpredictability becomes the ordinary condition of educational planning, the design principles documented here, that is, diverse pre-class materials plus interactive live sessions, transfer directly to the new normal.

Speculation about AI and robots in higher education is abundant; grounded speculation is rarer. This study used a literature-based design fiction methodology to keep imagined futures anchored in existing scholarship. A systematic review of peer-reviewed work on AI, robotics, and higher education identified the field's central themes, which were then synthesized into three design fictions, each depicting a plausible future under different degrees of AI and robot integration. Analyzing the fictions side by side revealed where their implications converge and diverge for curriculum, pedagogy, learning outcomes, faculty roles, and institutional structures. The potential is substantial: personalized learning pathways, automated administration, powerful analytical tools. The hazards are equally structural, including data privacy, the ethics of autonomous systems, new digital literacies that institutions have not yet defined, and the possibility of displacement or skill obsolescence among educators. The conclusion resists both hype and alarm. The systematic review stage anchored the fictions in peer-reviewed literature on AI, robotics, and higher education, and each fiction was built to a different integration level by design. Realizing the benefits while containing the risks demands proactive strategic planning, serious ethical frameworks, and continuous professional development, none of which will emerge on their own.

What does it actually take for artificial intelligence to work in further education? This study approached the question from the supply side, examining drivers, barriers, and the business models of the EdTech companies building AI products. A systematic review of academic databases and industry reports was combined with interviews of 25 executives and product managers at leading AI-focused EdTech firms. The drivers are the familiar ones: personalized learning, administrative efficiency, wider accessibility. The barriers are more decisive in practice, namely data privacy concerns, faculty resistance, high implementation costs, and weak digital infrastructure. Three business models dominate the market: subscription access to AI tools, institutional partnership arrangements, and API-driven integration services. Successful AI integration, the analysis suggests, is not a procurement decision but a strategy spanning infrastructure, pedagogical redesign, ethics, and financial sustainability. Industry reports were analyzed alongside academic databases, and the twenty-five interviewees held executive or product roles at AI-focused firms. It also requires policymakers, educational leaders, and EdTech innovators to cooperate rather than simply transact, since none of them controls enough of the equation alone.

Can a chatbot improve learning in a team-based design course, where problems are open-ended and support needs are constant? This quasi-experiment with 120 undergraduate engineering students tested exactly that. The experimental cohort (n=60) worked with an AI-powered chatbot providing real-time feedback, knowledge support, and collaborative assistance throughout their design projects; the control cohort (n=60) followed standard project-based learning. Data came from project grades, a validated learning outcomes questionnaire, and thematic analysis of student reflections. Chatbot users earned significantly higher project grades (p < 0.01) and reported stronger perceived learning, particularly in problem-solving and critical thinking. Their reflections added texture to the numbers: collaboration within teams improved, and cognitive load felt lighter with a responsive assistant absorbing routine questions. Project grades, the validated questionnaire, and reflection themes were analyzed as three independent evidence streams, and all three converged. Team-level dynamics also improved measurably across the semester. Chatbots will not replace the pedagogy of project-based learning, nor should they, but as supplementary tools in complex, team-based design courses they earn their place, improving outcomes while enriching the experience.

Early warning systems in universities typically flag struggling students after the struggle is visible. This study built an AI framework that moves the warning earlier. Using records from 10,000 students across five academic years, spanning academic histories, engagement metrics, and demographics, we combined an LSTM neural network for sequential analysis of academic progression with a Random Forest classifier for isolating the factors behind decline. After training, validation, and testing (evaluated with precision, recall, F1, and AUC), the hybrid model identified at-risk students up to a month in advance with 89.5% accuracy, comfortably ahead of traditional early warning systems. The telltale signals were mundane and therefore useful: slipping assignment scores, reduced LMS activity, declining attendance. On each prediction, the system suggested tailored responses, from tutoring referrals to counseling sessions to peer mentoring. The dataset spanned five academic years and included academic histories, engagement metrics, and demographics for all 10,000 students. The LSTM handled the sequential progression data while the Random Forest isolated decline factors, and the standard train-validate-test split with precision, recall, F1, and AUC evaluation kept the 89.5% figure honest. Intervention suggestions were generated per prediction rather than as generic advice. AI-driven monitoring of this kind is both effective and scalable, giving institutions the one thing conventional systems rarely provide: time to intervene before underperformance hardens into failure.

For online students, engagement is less a state than a balancing act, and this study set out to understand how they manage it. Twenty-five undergraduates in fully online programs at a large public university, purposively sampled for disciplinary and experiential diversity, participated in semi-structured interviews analyzed through a constructivist grounded theory approach. The balancing act has several fronts at once: negotiating what technology enables and obstructs, carrying the weight of self-directed learning, sustaining interaction with instructors and peers, and holding onto motivation against a background of potential isolation. Instructor presence and thoughtful pedagogical design emerged as the strongest facilitators. Focus and procrastination were the most common private struggles, and students differed widely in how actively they sought out social and academic connection. Effective online environments, the findings suggest, cannot rely on tools alone. The constructivist grounded theory approach meant categories were built from the interview data rather than imposed, and purposive sampling ensured disciplinary and experiential diversity across the twenty-five participants. They must deliberately cultivate community, provide clear structure, and equip students with self-regulation strategies, because the demands of online learning are ultimately managed by the student, hour by hour.

Online learning platforms are frequently described as supplements to higher education. This study argues they have become something else: structural forces reconstructing it. A mixed-methods design combined quantitative analysis of enrollment and completion across platform models, including MOOCs, blended formats, and fully online degrees, with interviews of 60 administrators, faculty, and students at five institutions using such platforms extensively. The shift is toward flexible, accessible, personalized pathways: platforms are reaching broader student demographics and enabling competency-based modules that conventional structures handle awkwardly. The strains are equally visible in digital equity gaps, faculty insufficiently trained for platform-mediated teaching, and persistent worries about academic rigor online. Reading the two together, platforms emerge not as add-ons but as drivers reshaping curriculum design, assessment strategy, and institutional infrastructure simultaneously. Higher education's choice is narrowing to adaptation on its own terms or adaptation on the platforms' terms, and the equity gaps will not close as a side effect of either.

Punctuation is a stubborn weak spot in university students' Spanish writing, and conventional instruction has not fixed it. This study tested a chatbot instead. In a quasi-experimental design, 120 undergraduates were split between an experimental group using a conversational agent for self-directed punctuation practice and a control group receiving traditional instruction. Pre- and post-tests measured proficiency; surveys and open feedback captured how students experienced the tool. The experimental group improved significantly more (p < 0.01). Just as telling was what students said: the immediate feedback kept them motivated, the self-paced format gave them autonomy, and access to practice whenever they wanted made learning feel genuinely flexible, which is precisely what open and flexible learning models promise and often fail to deliver. A chatbot will not teach everything, but for targeted skills like punctuation it works, and it does so while making the learning experience more accessible and personal. Pre- and post-tests bracketed the intervention for both groups, and the survey and open feedback were collected from the experimental group throughout. The proficiency gain and the experiential account therefore rest on separate instruments. That combination deserves a place in language programs moving toward open educational models.

Online courses log two kinds of showing up: joining live sessions and working through materials on one's own time. Which matters more for grades? Records from 2,548 students in twelve fully online courses at a large public university (2022-2023) were analyzed with multiple linear regression, with attendance data from the LMS separated into synchronous session participation and asynchronous engagement with recorded lectures and discussion boards, controlling for prior GPA and student classification. Both forms of attendance predicted final grades positively and significantly. Synchronous attendance carried slightly more unique weight (β = 0.38, p < .001) than asynchronous engagement (β = 0.31, p < .001), suggesting real-time interaction adds a margin that recordings do not fully replace. The practical conclusion is not to abandon flexibility, which remains one of online education's genuine strengths, but to actively encourage live participation within it. Attendance data were extracted directly from the LMS rather than self-reported, and synchronous and asynchronous engagement were operationalized as separate predictors in the same regression. Controlling for prior GPA and student classification isolated the attendance effects from ability differences. Course designs that make synchronous sessions worth attending, rather than merely available, are likely to convert that margin into achievement.

Initial enthusiasm for a learning technology tells you little; what matters is whether students still accept it after months of real use. This study measured acceptance of four digital learning technologies, namely classroom response systems, classroom chat, e-lectures, and mobile virtual reality, after three months of consistent usage. A UTAUT2-based survey of 450 students across disciplines was paired with 30 interviews. The four technologies fared very differently. E-lectures sustained the highest acceptance, fitting neatly into existing study habits and earning their perceived usefulness. Response systems landed in the middle: valued for immediate feedback, undermined by technical glitches. Classroom chat fell lower, more often experienced as distraction than support. Mobile VR told the most cautionary tale, as strong initial enjoyment eroded under effort demands and access problems. Sustained acceptance, the pattern suggests, is won at the intersection of functional utility, user experience, and compatibility with how students already work. The UTAUT2 survey was administered after three months of consistent use by design, so the acceptance scores reflect settled rather than novelty-driven judgments. The thirty interviews sampled users of all four technologies, and the qualitative accounts explain each technology's trajectory, including VR's decline from enthusiasm to abandonment. Novelty opens the door; only routine integration keeps a technology inside.

The Community of Inquiry framework rests on three presences, namely social, cognitive, and teaching, and online courses struggle with each in characteristic ways. This systematic review synthesized 78 peer-reviewed studies (2013-2023, from Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC) using qualitative content analysis to map how the presences are conceptualized, how they surface in practice, and how they depend on one another. A clear asymmetry emerged. Cognitive presence is the one courses most explicitly target, yet its development leans heavily on the other two, and those are precisely where the persistent difficulties lie: learners who do not feel connected to each other, discussion that stays shallow rather than becoming critical discourse, and instructor guidance or feedback that arrives too thin or too late. Treating the presences separately therefore misreads the framework. What the evidence supports is a holistic approach that cultivates all three deliberately and together. Qualitative content analysis coded how each presence was conceptualized, how it surfaced in practice, and how the presences depended on one another across the 78 studies. The decade window captured the framework's mature application period. Dynamic models for assessing the presences, especially across cultural and technological contexts, stand out as the field's next requirement.

Open educational resources promise education for everyone, but 'everyone' has too often excluded disabled learners. This systematic review examined the state of accessibility in OER and open educational practices, following PRISMA guidelines across Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and Google Scholar and appraising 47 peer-reviewed articles from 2010-2023. Awareness of accessibility is growing; implementation lags well behind it. Technical barriers persist, including missing alternative text, poor color contrast, and interfaces that cannot be navigated by assistive technology, alongside pedagogical ones such as inflexible learning pathways and thin support for diverse learning needs, with accessibility rarely anchored at the policy level. The encouraging findings cluster around a different way of working: co-creating resources with disabled learners, applying universal design for learning principles from the start, and institutional commitment to accessible development rather than retrofit. The PRISMA protocol governed searching and screening across all four databases, and the 47 articles were appraised for both technical and pedagogical accessibility dimensions. Policy-level anchoring was coded separately, which is how its near-absence became visible. Genuinely inclusive open education requires accessibility to be embedded across the whole OER lifecycle, supported by policy frameworks, developer training, and user-centered design research, not appended once the resources are built.

Educational videos are everywhere in higher education, yet what makes students actually use them, and does using them satisfy? This study extended the Technology Acceptance Model to find out, surveying 450 undergraduates across disciplines and testing the model with structural equation modeling. The instrument covered perceived usefulness, ease of use, self-efficacy, instructor support, system quality, video usage, and learning satisfaction. Usefulness, ease of use, and self-efficacy all directly predicted video usage. Instructor support and system quality mattered too, but indirectly, with support working through perceived usefulness and quality through ease of use. Usage, in turn, significantly raised learning satisfaction. The pattern refines rather than overturns TAM: the core constructs hold, but they are fed by external conditions that instructors and institutions control. A well-supported student facing a well-built system finds videos more useful and easier to use, uses them more, and is more satisfied with learning as a result. Measurement validity was established before the structural model was run, and the sample's disciplinary spread guards against single-field effects. The indirect paths for instructor support and system quality were estimated within the full model, so the mediation claims rest on simultaneous rather than piecewise testing. For instructional designers, those two levers, meaning support and system quality, are the actionable part of the chain.

MOOC discussion forums are where peer learning is supposed to happen; whether it does, and for whom, is what this study examined. Forum activity from 1,247 participants across three MOOCs was analyzed with correlation and regression against final grades, followed by thematic analysis of 86 purposively selected threads and interviews with 28 high- and low-performing students. Three factors consistently predicted engagement in peer learning: the quality and frequency of peer feedback, how relevant students found the discussion prompts, and their own self-regulation strategies. One finding deserves emphasis: threads containing a greater diversity of perspectives were associated with better performance, suggesting that encountering disagreement and difference does real cognitive work. The negative side of the ledger was familiar, encompassing delayed responses, absent instructors, and the perception that others were coasting. Peer learning in asynchronous forums, then, is not self-organizing. The 86 threads were purposively selected to span the three MOOCs and performance levels, and the 28 interviewees included both high and low performers. Regression linked forum behavior to final grades before the qualitative phase explained the mechanisms. It responds to design, through carefully constructed prompts, timely moderation, and explicit norms for constructive feedback, and where those are provided, forum participation translates into performance.

Educational virtual reality games have accumulated a research literature large enough to take stock of, and this systematic review does so for 2018-2023. Searches across Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ACM Digital Library yielded 87 peer-reviewed studies meeting the inclusion criteria; extraction covered study design, game characteristics, measured outcomes, and participant demographics. The field's shape is distinct. STEM subjects dominate, quasi-experimental comparisons with traditional instruction are the modal design, and gamified simulations and interactive storytelling are the prevailing formats across K-12 and higher education. Cognitive engagement and motivation are the outcomes most reliably improved; evidence on long-term knowledge retention remains genuinely mixed. Haptic feedback and multi-user environments mark the current design frontier. The overall verdict is promise with caveats. Extraction covered study design, game characteristics, measured outcomes, and participant demographics for every included study, and the four-database search kept coverage broad. The 2018-2023 window captures the field's most active period.
